crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: FAIR Data
children.blurb: FAIR Data is a set of guiding principles for making research data Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable.

children.name: Metadata and Ontologies
children.blurb: Metadata and ontologies in research data and repositories cover the structured descriptions that make data, papers, models, and tools discoverable and the formal vocabularies that give those descriptions shared meaning.

children.name: Federated Sharing of Sensitive Data
children.blurb: Federated sharing of sensitive data covers arrangements where two or more organisations analyse data that cannot be pooled in one place, such as patient records, genomic sequences, financial transactions or personal device data.

children.name: Institutional Knowledge Graphs
children.blurb: Institutional knowledge graphs represent the entities an organization cares about, such as people, projects, publications, datasets, instruments, and administrative units, and the relationships among them.

children.name: Long-Term Digital Preservation
children.blurb: Long-term digital preservation is the work of keeping digital objects usable, understandable, and trustworthy over decades, across changes in hardware, software, formats, and organizations.

sections.body: Research data and repositories is the part of AI research infrastructure that deals with how data is described, stored, shared, and kept usable over time. AI is not just a consumer of these repositories; it is increasingly used to create and maintain them. Machine learning models extract metadata from papers and datasets, align terms across ontologies, resolve author and institution names, and build links between records that humans would otherwise miss. In practice this means a repository can turn a pile of files into a searchable graph of datasets, methods, and claims. The work is less about a single clever model and more about pipelines that combine text extraction, schema matching, and human review. The goal is to make data findable and reusable without losing the context that makes it meaningful.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts are mature. Persistent identifiers, standard metadata schemas, and repository software are widely used, and FAIR principles have become a common reference point. What is not solved is the messy middle: metadata is often incomplete, inconsistent, or locked in PDFs and spreadsheets. Ontology alignment remains hard because different communities use different terms for similar concepts, and automated matches still need expert checking. Federated sharing of sensitive data is technically possible but constrained by law, ethics, and institutional policy, not just by algorithms, and long-term preservation is also unresolved in practice because formats change, software decays, and funding for maintenance is rarely secure. AI can help at the edges, but it does not remove the need for governance, curation, and stable institutions.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages in this section follow the life of research data from description to durability. FAIR Data sets out the principles and the practical tests for findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable records. Metadata and Ontologies goes deeper into the schemas and vocabularies that make machine reasoning possible, including the glossary terms that anchor shared meaning. Federated Sharing of Sensitive Data addresses the harder case where data cannot be pooled in one place and must be queried across sites under controls. Institutional Knowledge Graphs shows how an organisation can connect its own papers, models, tools, and people into a navigable structure, which is where a library of 135 research papers and 13608 claims extracted from research works becomes more than a list. Long-Term Digital Preservation closes the section by asking what survives when the original software and formats are gone, and a reader would go to each page for a different layer of the same problem: principles, description, controlled sharing, institutional integration, and time.
